source_text: Si non audieritis, visitabo in virga. Castigatio misericors. Revertere.
orientation: Origen is expounding the covenant blessings and curses of Leviticus 26, now turning to God's warning of punishment for those who do not hear.
pass_a_gloss: If you will not have heard, I will visit in a rod. Merciful chastisement. Turn back.

choices.english: If you will not have heard
choices.why: Keeps the future perfect force of the Latin, matching the conditional warning in Leviticus 26.

choices.english: I will visit in a rod
choices.why: Preserves the literal 'visit' and the instrumental 'in a rod', echoing the biblical idiom of divine visitation for punishment.
rejected: I will punish with a rod
I will come with a rod

choices.why: Renders the noun phrase as a heading-like summary, matching Origen's homiletic style of naming the section's theme.
The imperative singular addresses the hearer directly, preserving the call to conversion.

pass_b_english: If you will not have heard, I will visit in a rod (Leviticus 26:14, 16). Merciful chastisement. Turn back.

last_rejected.quote: If you will not have heard, I will visit in a rod (Leviticus 26:14, 16).
last_rejected.source_quote: Si non audieritis, visitabo in virga.
last_rejected.why: English hides that this is God speaking; source is divine first-person threat.
last_rejected.fix: If you will not listen, I will punish you with the rod, says the Lord.
last_rejected.ruling: First-person 'visitabo' is preserved; English doesn't hide divine speaker. No error.

last_rejected.why: "Visit" alone is archaic/weak; "in virga" means "with a rod" (instrumental).
last_rejected.ruling: 'Visit in a rod' is literal KJV-style; 'in' can be instrumental. Within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: If you will not have heard
last_rejected.why: Future perfect misrepresents Latin future perfect as completed action; should be simple future condition.
last_rejected.ruling: Future perfect is standard for Latin future perfect in conditional clauses; not a mistranslation.

last_rejected.why: Latin is a complete clause/claim about the nature of chastisement; English renders as fragment losing force.
last_rejected.ruling: Both Latin and English are phrases, not full clauses; no omission or meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: Latin is imperative command; English "Turn back" is ambiguous as imperative vs noun phrase.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Turn back' is clearly imperative in context, matching 'revertere'; no real ambiguity.
